title: Magnets & Electromagnets - Application
welcome_lead: Wire up an electromagnet and bring magnets to life.

concepts.def: Magnet made by current in a coil.
Coil of wire with a magnetic field.
Iron bar inside coil; boosts strength.
Electromagnet rings a bell when pressed.

walkthroughs.body_html:
A simple electromagnet:

1. Wrap a wire around an iron nail in a coil.
2. Connect to a battery.
3. Current flows - the nail becomes a magnet!

Disconnect the battery, and it stops being magnetic.

Unlike a normal magnet, an electromagnet is switchable.

To boost an electromagnet:

More turns in the coil.
More current through the wire.
Iron core instead of plastic.

Stronger electromagnets can lift heavier objects - scrapyard cranes carry whole car wrecks!

Electromagnets are everywhere:

Scrapyard cranes - pick up and drop iron with a switch.
Doorbells - magnetic plunger hits a bell.
Electric motors - in fans, drills, trains.
Maglev trains - float above the track on magnets.
Loudspeakers - vibrate cones to make sound.

mcqs.q: What is the main advantage of an electromagnet over a normal magnet?
options: It's cheaper
It can be switched on and off
It never demagnetises
It needs no power

mcqs.q: Which would NOT make an electromagnet stronger?
options: More turns of wire
Higher current
Iron core
Plastic core

mcqs.q: Which of the following is a fundamental particle: proton, electron, or neutron?
options: The mass of the object creating the field.
All three (proton, electron, neutron) are fundamental particles that cannot be broken down.
Only the electron — protons and neutrons are made of quarks.
Only the proton is fundamental; electrons and neutrons are composite.

mcqs.q: What does gravitational field strength at a point represent?
options: The mass of the object creating the field.
The total gravitational force at that point regardless of mass.
The force per unit mass that would act on a test mass placed at that point.
Only the proton is fundamental; electrons and neutrons are composite.
